reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Common variable enteropathy is a chronic non-infective enteropathy of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), presenting with chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss despite immunoglobulin replacement.

Histology often resembles coeliac disease with villous atrophy, but characteristically shows a paucity or absence of lamina propria plasma cells and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and does not respond to a gluten-free diet.
Other patterns include lymphoid nodular hyperplasia, a graft-versus-host-like appearance and changes resembling inflammatory bowel disease; gastric involvement may cause atrophic gastritis.
Treatable infective mimics such as Giardia, cytomegalovirus, Cryptosporidium, small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth and Campylobacter must be excluded first.
IgA-based coeliac serology is unreliable in antibody deficiency, so diagnosis rests on histology and exclusion of infection rather than serology.

The enteropathy is associated with other non-infective CVID complications, including nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, autoimmune cytopenias and an increased lymphoma risk.
Immunoglobulin replacement corrects infection risk but does not treat the enteropathy; corticosteroids (including budesonide) and steroid-sparing immunomodulators are used for refractory disease.
Nutritional support and surveillance for gastric carcinoma and lymphoma are important components of long-term care.
reference.pathophysiology: The enteropathy reflects the dysregulated mucosal immunity of CVID rather than a single mechanism. Deficient B-cell differentiation and a striking reduction in mucosal plasma cells impair local secretory antibody, while T-cell dysregulation, aberrant innate immune signalling and an altered gut microbiome contribute to immune-mediated small-bowel injury. The result is villous atrophy and chronic inflammation histologically overlapping with coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, but distinguished by the paucity of plasma cells. Chronic infection and immune dysregulation coexist, and the same immune defects underlie the systemic non-infective complications seen in CVID.
additionalDifferentials: giardiasis and other chronic gastrointestinal infections
inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn's disease
additionalInvestigations: quantitative immunoglobulins and vaccine responses to establish CVID
duodenal and colonic biopsies for villous atrophy and reduced plasma cells
stool microscopy and antigen testing for Giardia and Cryptosporidium with stool culture
cytomegalovirus PCR and immunohistochemistry on biopsy
nutritional panel including iron, B12, folate and fat-soluble vitamins
cross-sectional imaging or enteroscopy and a hydrogen breath test for bacterial overgrowth
redFlags: rapid weight loss or severe malabsorption
refractory diarrhoea despite treatment of identified infection
features suggesting lymphoma such as a mass, night sweats or rising LDH
hepatosplenomegaly or signs of portal hypertension from nodular regenerative hyperplasia
reference.prognosis: The course is variable but often chronic and difficult to treat, and the enteropathy is associated with poorer outcomes in CVID and with increased risks of lymphoma and malnutrition.
pitfalls: relying on coeliac serology in an antibody-deficient patient
assuming villous atrophy equals coeliac disease and prescribing a gluten-free diet
missing treatable infection such as Giardia or cytomegalovirus
attributing symptoms solely to CVID without obtaining biopsies
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Continue immunoglobulin replacement (intravenous or subcutaneous) as the backbone of CVID care, recognising it controls infection but does not reliably reverse the enteropathy

Exclude and treat infective mimics before immunosuppression - antiparasitic therapy for Giardia and Cryptosporidium, antiviral therapy for cytomegalovirus, antibiotics for Campylobacter, and directed antibiotics for small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth
For biopsy-proven immune-mediated enteropathy, use corticosteroids including the topically-acting agent budesonide, escalating to immunomodulators or biologic therapy in refractory disease
Avoid reliance on a gluten-free diet, which does not help this plasma-cell-poor villous atrophy despite the coeliac-like histology
Provide nutritional support with replacement of iron, vitamin B12, folate and fat-soluble vitamins, and dietetic input for malabsorption and weight loss
Undertake surveillance for associated CVID complications - nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, autoimmune cytopenias and lymphoma
Manage through a joint gastroenterology and clinical immunology multidisciplinary team
